Hi there—thank you for taking a few minutes to talk with me. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal-mental-health clinician who works with new moms to be sure they’re getting the emotional support they deserve.  

Today we’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s a well-studied tool that helps us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and any thoughts of self-harm that can sometimes show up after a baby is born. The goal is simply to understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can make sure you have the right care and resources.  

Everything you share is confidential; only the scoring and any safety concerns would be shared with your medical team. We’ll go through ten questions, and I’ll ask each one in everyday language—no need to remember numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we can begin.  

Let’s start: in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has that been difficult for you?

I… I haven’t really felt like myself. Even the little things I used to like—watching a show, texting friends—just feel kind of pointless. I can still smile if someone shows me a cute video or if the baby coos, but the happiness doesn’t last.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I do laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent that silly meme—but it feels kind of forced, and the giggles fade fast. Most of the time I’m too worn-out or worried to find much funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels like another chore. I’ll tell myself “I should want to do this,” but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s something I ate or that I’m not soothing him right. When I couldn’t get the swaddle tight enough last night, I sat on the edge of the crib crying, telling myself I’m already failing him. I know, rationally, babies just cry—but the guilt still barges in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

All the time. Even when everything looks fine—he’s breathing, sleeping, no fever—I still hover over the crib or keep checking the monitor. My heart races like something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week it hit me out of nowhere. I’ll be folding his tiny onesies and suddenly my chest tightens, I feel shaky, and I have to sit down because I’m sure something terrible is about to happen—even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. Between the night feedings, the constant laundry, and trying to keep track of his diapers, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Sometimes I just stare at the mess and think, “I’ll never catch up,” and the tears start before I can stop them.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head spins with everything I think I did wrong that day—did I burp him long enough, did I miss a dirty diaper—and I can’t shut it off. Some nights I’m still awake when he wakes up again, and then I’m too teary to fall back asleep even after he’s settled.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel this heavy sadness settle in. I look at his little face and think, “I should be glowing,” but instead I feel hollow and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three or four times since last weekend. Yesterday it was because I spilled the pumped milk on the counter—just stood there sobbing like I’d ruined everything. The tears come fast, and once they start it’s hard to turn them off.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed and cry, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can be the mom he deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: New mother, 1–2 weeks post-delivery (no self-harm ideation endorsed)

Key Symptoms / Behaviors reported  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, “hollow” feelings (daily)  
- Marked anhedonia—no interest/enjoyment in previously pleasant activities  
- Excessive, intrusive guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Chronic, unprovoked anxiety, heart racing, “shaky” panic episodes  
- Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia ruminating about parenting “mistakes”)  
- Frequent crying spells, feeling “overwhelmed,” unable to “catch up”  
- Fatigue and sense of emotional depletion  
- Maintained appetite; no suicidal thoughts

Pattern Consistency  
All ten items endorsed at clinically significant levels; highest severity on mood, guilt, anxiety, coping.

Screening Significance  
- Meets threshold indicators for probable Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset (DSM-5 specifier)  
- Co-occurring anxiety/panic symptoms exceed typical “baby blues” expectations  
- Functional impact evident (difficulty completing infant care tasks, emotional availability)

Risk Factors Highlighted  
- Daily crying, pervasive sadness >2 weeks  
- Loss of pleasure/enjoyment  
- Sleep disruption linked to mood rather than infant demands alone  
- Excessive guilt/worthlessness  
- Panic-type episodes without identifiable trigger  
- NO suicidal/homicidal ideation reported (safety risk: absent at present)

Observation  
Screening findings suggest elevated risk for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; recommend prompt formal evaluation by licensed mental-health provider and coordination with OB/pediatric team for further assessment and possible treatment referral.
